title: Introduction to Computer Networks
tagline: Why networks exist, how the Internet is built, and the vocabulary — delay, throughput, switching, devices & layers — that every later lecture builds on.
summary: The complete ground floor of networking: what a network is made of, how the global Internet grew out of small local networks, how data moves (switching), how we measure "speed" (delay, latency, throughput), which devices do which job, and the two layer models used to talk about it all — with worked numericals and exam questions.
objectives: Explain why networks exist and identify their building blocks (nodes & links)
Classify networks by scale: PAN, LAN, MAN, WAN — with real examples
Describe the Internet as a "network of networks" organised in ISP tiers
Separate the network edge from the network core and name what lives in each
Contrast circuit switching and packet switching, and argue why the Internet chose packets
Compute nodal delay (processing, queueing, transmission, propagation) and throughput from formulas
Pick the right device (hub, switch, router, modem) for a given job
Read the OSI (7-layer) and TCP/IP (4/5-layer) models at a bird's-eye level

sections.title: Why Computer Networks?
sections.html:
A computer network is a set of devices (called nodes) connected by communication channels (called links) that exchange data. That's the entire definition — everything else in this course is detail on top of it.

Nodes — the devices
Computers, laptops, phones, servers, printers, and the networking boxes themselves: routers, switches, hubs. Any device that can send, receive, or forward data.
Links — the connections
Wired (copper twisted pair, fiber optic) or wireless (Wi-Fi radio, cellular, satellite). A link carries signals that encode bits.

Why do we need them?

  • Communication — humans and programs talking across a room or across the planet (chat, email, calls, web).
  • Resource sharing — one printer for an office, one file server for a team, one database for a million users.
  • Scale — work distributed across machines: cloud computing, search engines, video streaming at planetary scale.
  • Cost & reliability — shared infrastructure and replicated systems beat every user owning everything.
Analogy
The classic mental model: the postal system. A letter (data) is placed in an envelope (packet) with an address (destination IP), handed to a post office (router), and forwarded office-by-office until it reaches the mailbox (destination device). No single postal worker knows the whole journey — each just knows the next office. This is exactly how Internet routing works (Lecture 7).
Big Picture
Everything you use daily — WhatsApp, UPI payments, YouTube, Instagram, exam results websites — is a program on one machine talking to programs on other machines through this stack of ideas. Master these 13 lectures and you can explain every step of what happens when you type a URL (Lecture 13 does exactly that).

sections.html:
Networks are classified by geographic scale. The scale decides the technology, ownership, speed and cost.

MANMetropolitan Area NetworkA cityISP / large orgModerateCable TV network, city-wide ISP backbone, metro college campuses joined

Figure 1. Networks grow from personal to planetary — bigger scale means more owners, more hops, more latency.
Exam
A favourite short-answer: "Differentiate LAN and WAN." Key points: LAN = small area, privately owned, high speed, low latency; WAN = huge area, owned by telecom providers (leased links), moderate speed, higher latency and cost. Give one example of each.
Note
The Internet is not one WAN — it is millions of LANs and WANs interconnected: a network of networks. A VPN (Virtual Private Network) is a secure tunnel built on top of the Internet to make a remote machine behave as if it is on your LAN.

sections.title: Internet Architecture — the Network of Networks
sections.html:
No single company owns the Internet. It grew by connecting smaller networks (ISPs) into a loose global hierarchy:

Figure 2. The Internet hierarchy: Tier-1 carriers form the core; regional and local ISPs bring access networks to your device.
  • Tier-1 ISPs own long-distance fiber backbones and peer with each other as equals — they never pay anyone for transit.
  • Tier-2 / regional ISPs buy connectivity from Tier-1s and sell to smaller networks.
  • Access networks (Tier-3) — local ISPs, mobile towers, campus networks — connect the last metres to your device.
  • Content providers (Google, Netflix, Cloudflare) run their own global networks and data centers, connecting into this hierarchy at many points (and via CDNs — Lecture 13).
Exam
"What is meant by the Internet being a network of networks?" — Answer shape: end systems connect into access ISPs (LAN, then ISP); access ISPs connect into regional ISPs; regional into Tier-1 backbone ISPs; smaller networks at each level are themselves networks of routers and links. Nobody owns the whole; interoperability comes from shared protocols (TCP/IP).

sections.title: Network Edge vs Network Core
sections.html:
Figure 3. Edge devices reach the core through an access link; the core is a cooperating mesh of routers running packet switching.
Network Edge
End systems: PCs, phones, servers, IoT devices. Hosts = clients (requesters: your browser) and servers (responders: Google's machines). Edge devices run applications.
Network Core
A mesh of interconnected routers. Its only job: move data — millions of packets per second, from any edge to any other edge. Contains no applications; pure forwarding machinery.
Exam
"With a neat diagram, explain network edge and network core." Draw Figure 3. Edge = hosts + access networks (Wi-Fi, FTTH, DSL, cellular). Core = router mesh doing packet switching. One line each on client/server and on why the core is shared.

sections.title: Circuit Switching vs Packet Switching
sections.html:
How does the core carry data for many conversations at once? Two historical answers:

Circuit Switching — the telephone way
Reserve a dedicated end-to-end path first ( signalling sets up the "circuit"), then send at fixed rate. Links are divided into channels by FDM (frequency-division: each call gets a frequency band) or TDM (time-division: each call gets repeating time slots).
  • Guaranteed constant rate & latency — perfect for voice.
  • Wasteful: silent moments (pauses in a call) still hold the circuit.
  • Setup time before any data; fails if any intermediate trunk is busy.
Packet Switching — the Internet way
No reservation. Data is chopped into packets (a few KB each) with headers; each router forwards them using store-and-forward: receive the whole packet, check it, send it on the next link. Packets from many users statistically share every link.
  • Efficient sharing — idle capacity is instantly reused.
  • Resilient: packets simply reroute around failures.
  • No guarantees — congestion causes queueing delay and loss.
Figure 4. Circuit switching reserves a fixed channel end-to-end; packet switching forwards self-contained packets over shared links.

Numerical: why packets win on efficiency

Users share a 1 Mbps link. Each user is active 10% of the time and needs 100 kbps when active.
Circuit switching: each user must reserve 100 kbps forever → only 1 Mbps ÷ 100 kbps = 10 users, and the link sits 90% idle for each of them.
Packet switching (n users): each user active with p = 0.1. Probability that more than 10 are active simultaneously: P(>10 active) = Σ k=11..n C(n,k) (0.1)k(0.9)n−k. For n = 35, this is under 0.04% — so packet switching supports ~35 users on the same link with essentially no congestion.
Total store-and-forward delay over N links = N × (L / R)
L = packet size in bits · R = link rate in bps — each link must fully receive the packet before retransmitting it
Numerical
Classic exam numerical: Send a 1,000-bit packet over two 1 Mbps links (store-and-forward). Total time = 2 × (1000 / 10⁶) = 2 ms. (First link: 1 ms to push it out; second router waits until it has all 1000 bits, then 1 ms more.) With a single 1 Mbps link it would be just 1 ms — each extra hop adds L/R.
Why the Internet chose packets
Data traffic is bursty (long silences, sudden bursts). Reserving capacity for the silence wastes it; statistical sharing exploits it. Result: cheaper, scalable, resilient — at the cost of congestion management, which TCP handles later (Lecture 10).

sections.title: Delay & Latency — the Four Delays
sections.html:
Every packet suffers delays at every router hop. Total nodal delay has exactly four components:

Figure 5. The delay pipeline every packet passes through at each hop.
DelayWhat happensFormulaDepends onTypical size
ProcessingRouter examines header, checks bit errors, looks up output linkd_procRouter hardware speedMicroseconds — usually ignored
QueueingPacket waits in the output buffer while earlier packets are sentd_queueTraffic intensity (how busy the link is)0 when idle → grows unboundedly near congestion
TransmissionAll L bits of the packet are pushed onto the wired_trans = L / RPacket length L, link rate Rms scale for big packets on slow links
PropagationThe signal physically travels the medium's lengthd_prop = d / sDistance d, propagation speed s ≈ 2×10⁸ m/s (fiber/copper)~5 ms per 1000 km — physics, can't be upgraded!
Trap
Transmission ≠ Propagation. Transmission is writing bits onto the link (rate-limited by bandwidth); propagation is the signal racing along the wire (limited by physics). A 10-lane highway on-ramp analogy: transmission = how fast cars enter (one per second); propagation = how fast a car drives to the next city.

Worked example — compute all four delays

Given: packet length L = 1000 bytes, link rate R = 10 Mbps, link length d = 1000 km, propagation speed s = 2 × 10⁸ m/s, queueing delay ≈ 0 (link idle), processing ≈ 0.
1
Convert units first
L = 1000 B × 8 = 8000 bits; R = 10 Mbps = 10⁷ bps; d = 1000 km = 10⁶ m
2
Transmission delay
d_trans = L/R = 8000 / 10⁷ = 8×10⁻⁴ s = 0.8 ms
3
Propagation delay
d_prop = d/s = 10⁶ / (2×10⁸) = 5×10⁻³ s = 5 ms
4
Total nodal delay
d_nodal ≈ 0 + 0 + 0.8 + 5 = 5.8 ms — here propagation dominates

Queueing delay & traffic intensity

Traffic intensity ρ = (a · L) / R
a = average packet arrival rate (packets/s) · L = average packet size · R = link rate
Traffic intensity ρWhat happens to average queueing delay
ρ ≪ 1Arrivals are rare — packets rarely wait; average queueing delay ≈ 0
ρ → 1Delay grows rapidly and fluctuates wildly (bursts collide)
ρ > 1Arrivals exceed service rate — queue grows without bound → packets are dropped (loss)
Numerical
Practice: a = 1000 packets/s, L = 1000 bits, R = 2 Mbps → ρ = (1000×1000)/(2×10⁶) = 0.5: stable, moderate queueing. If a doubles to 2000 → ρ = 1: queue explodes. Design rule: keep ρ well below 1.

Latency vs RTT

  • Latency (one-way) = time for a packet to travel source → destination (all four delays summed over every hop).
  • RTT (Round-Trip Time) = there and back. Ping reports RTT (Lecture 12). Bengaluru → US server ≈ 200–250 ms RTT.
  • Latency matters as much as bandwidth for interactive apps: gaming, video calls, web page loads.

sections.title: Bandwidth, Throughput & Bottlenecks
sections.html:
Bandwidth
The maximum rate a link can carry (bits/second). What your ISP advertises: "100 Mbps plan". Also called link capacity or rate R.
Throughput
The actual rate achieved end-to-end at an instant: bits/second successfully delivered. What your download bar shows.
Bottleneck link
The slowest link on the path — it alone caps the throughput. Fixing any other link changes nothing!
End-to-end throughput ≈ min(R₁, R₂, R₃, … Rₙ)
the path is a chain of links — water can't flow faster than the narrowest pipe
Figure 6. Bottleneck principle — upgrading R₁ (or your Wi-Fi) is pointless until the 2 Mbps link is fixed.
Analogy
A highway chain: 8-lane expressway (high bandwidth) feeding a single-lane village road (low bandwidth). Traffic arrives at the village rate no matter how wide the expressway is. Same with your 1 Gbps laptop NIC on a 20 Mbps broadband line.
Numerical
Path: server–R₁=30 Mbps → router –R₂=10 Mbps → ISP –R₃=50 Mbps → home. Throughput = min(30,10,50) = 10 Mbps. If ten clients share R₂ simultaneously and fairly, each gets ≈ 1 Mbps. Also note: delay and throughput interact — a 1 MB file's transfer time is roughly max(L/R_total, RTT-limited window growth) — revisited in Lecture 10 (sliding window).

sections.title: Network Devices — Hub, Switch, Router, Modem
sections.html:
Hub
Layer 1 · Physical
Dumb repeater: copies bits from one port to every other port. All devices share one collision domain and one bandwidth pool. Obsolete — but a favourite exam contrast.
Switch
Layer 2 · Data Link
Learns which MAC address lives on which port and forwards frames only to the right port. Each port gets full bandwidth; connects devices within one LAN.
Router
Layer 3 · Network
Connects different networks; forwards packets using IP addresses and a routing table. The only device that lives in the network core. Your "home router" is router + switch + more (Lecture 11).
Modem
Edge · Modulator
MOdulator-DEModulator: converts between your home's digital signals and your ISP's line format (DSL phone line, cable TV coax, fiber light). The bridge onto the Internet.
QuestionHubSwitchRouter
OSI layer1 — Physical2 — Data Link3 — Network
Addressing usedNone — electrical repeatMAC (hardware) addressesIP (logical) addresses
Forwarding decisionFloods to all portsMAC table lookup per portLongest-prefix match in routing table (L7)
ConnectsDevices in one segment (legacy)Devices within one LANDifferent networks (LAN ↔ Internet)
Intelligence / costNone · cheapestModerateHighest — runs routing protocols
Analogy
Hub = shouting in a room — everyone hears, only the addressee listens (chaos as crowd grows). Switch = an office receptionist who memorises faces (MACs) and hands each letter directly. Router = the postal system routing between cities (networks). Modem = the translator between your home's language and the ISP line's language.

sections.title: OSI vs TCP/IP — a Bird's-Eye View
sections.html:
Complex systems need layering: each layer does one job, serves the layer above, and uses the layer below. Two models organise the ideas — OSI (7 layers, the vocabulary) and TCP/IP (4 layers, what the Internet actually runs). Full detail arrives in Lecture 2; today, meet the shape:

Mnemonic — bottom to top
"Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away" → Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. (Top-down: "All People Seem To Need Data Processing".)
7ApplicationHTTP · DNS · SMTP — user-facing protocols
6Presentationformat, encryption — TLS lives here
5Sessiondialogue control, sessions
4TransportTCP · UDP — end-to-end delivery, ports
3NetworkIP — routing across networks
2Data LinkEthernet · Wi-Fi — frames, MAC addresses
1Physicalbits as voltages / light / radio
OSI model — 7 layers (ISO, 1984) — the reference vocabulary
4Applicationmerges OSI 5+6+7 — HTTP, DNS, TLS…
3TransportTCP · UDP
2InternetIP · ICMP — the network layer
1Network Accessmerges OSI 1+2 — Ethernet, Wi-Fi, 5G radio
TCP/IP model — 4 layers (DARPA) — what the Internet runs
Figure 7. Same ideas, different groupings: engineers implement TCP/IP but describe problems with OSI layer numbers ("that's a Layer 3 issue").
Exam
"Compare OSI and TCP/IP models." Points: OSI = 7 layers, theoretical reference, created by ISO for standardisation; TCP/IP = 4 (or 5) layers, practical, developed by DARPA, what the Internet actually uses. OSI's Session+Presentation collapse into TCP/IP's Application; OSI's Physical+Data Link collapse into Network Access. We implement TCP/IP but speak in OSI layer numbers.

A2. b — 1500 B = 12,000 bits ÷ 3×10⁶ = 4 ms.
A3. c — switch (L2, MAC table); hub floods, router uses IP.
A4. b — receive fully, then forward (adds L/R per hop).
A5. c — throughput = min link = 4 Mbps.
A6. Nodes = communicating devices; links = transmission media. Reasons: communication, resource sharing (any two: cost, reliability, scale).
A7. LAN: building/campus, privately owned, 100 Mbps–10 Gbps, very low latency (home Wi-Fi). WAN: country/world, telecom-owned leased links, higher latency & cost (Internet backbone, bank ATM network).
A8. Millions of interconnected networks; each access LAN → local ISP → regional → Tier-1; no single owner; common protocols bind them. (Sketch as in Figure 2.)
A9. Bandwidth = capacity of a link; throughput = achieved end-to-end rate = min of links; bottleneck = the slowest link. Example: 100 Mbps Wi-Fi → 10 Mbps broadband = 10 Mbps.
A10. Transmission = L/R (push bits on, upgradeable by buying bandwidth); propagation = d/s (physics of distance, not upgradeable).
A11. Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away. 5+6+7 → Application; 4 → Transport; 3 → Internet; 1+2 → Network Access.
A13. d_trans: 0.96 ms / 9.6 ms / 0.96 ms (L=9600 b). d_prop: 3 ms / 0.15 ms / 6 ms. Total = (0.96+9.6+0.96) + (3+0.15+6) = 20.67 ms — middle slow link dominates both terms.

A16. d_trans = 8000/10⁸ = 0.08 ms; d_prop = 2×10⁵/2×10⁸ = 1 ms; d_nodal ≈ 0 + 3 + 0.08 + 1 = 4.08 ms.

sections.title: What is a Protocol? Why Layers?
sections.html:
A protocol is a set of agreed-upon rules governing communication. Both sender and receiver must follow the same protocol or communication fails. In networking a protocol defines three things:

Format
Which fields appear, in what order, what each byte means (the message "grammar").
Sequence
Who initiates, who responds, and in what order (the "conversation flow").
Actions
What to do on events: message lost, corrupted, arrives out of order.

Why layered protocols?

Rather than one massive protocol doing everything, networking uses a layered architecture: each layer has one job, relies on the layer below, and provides a service to the layer above.

  • Modularity — change one layer without touching others: Apple can update Safari's HTTP engine without modifying TCP.
  • Reusability — TCP works identically over Ethernet, Wi-Fi, or 4G.
  • Isolation — easier diagnosis: if TCP connects but the page is broken, the problem is in the application layer, not the network.
Analogy
Sending a gift: you (application) write the card; the packing service (transport) boxes it; the courier company (network) routes the box; the local delivery van (data link) carries it on the final street; the road (physical) carries the van. Each level only cares about its own wrapping.

sections.title: The OSI Model — 7 Layers
sections.html:
In the 1980s vendors (IBM, DEC…) had incompatible systems. The ISO created the OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model, 1984, as a universal reference. Every network function belongs to one of 7 layers:

7Applicationrules for what apps say — HTTP · SMTP · DNS · SSH
6Presentationformatting, compression, encryption — TLS · JPEG · gzip
5Sessionsession lifecycle — largely absorbed into apps/TCP today
4Transportend-to-end delivery, ports, reliability — TCP · UDP
3Networkrouting across networks, IP addressing — IP · ICMP
2Data Linklocal delivery, frames, MAC — Ethernet · Wi-Fi 802.11
1Physicalbits on the wire — voltages · light · radio (Cat6, 802.11)
Layer numbers are used from TOP (7) to BOTTOM (1) — data flows 7→1 on send, 1→7 on receive
Figure 1. The OSI reference model — a common vocabulary, not a running implementation.
Mnemonic (bottom → top)
"Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away" → Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.
LayerOne-line jobIf it breaks… (symptom)

3 — NetworkRouting across networks via IP addressesCan reach your router but not the Internet
4 — TransportPort numbers (right application) + reliability (TCP / UDP)Connects but data corrupted, lost, or out of order
5 — SessionOpen / maintain / close sessions (handled by apps or TCP today)— (mostly historical)

Ethernet, Wi-Fi, LTE…
How we use both
We implement TCP/IP protocols, but talk about them with OSI layer numbers — "that's a Layer 3 problem", "an L2 switch". This course does the same: study TCP/IP protocols, use OSI numbers as vocabulary.
Note
Some textbooks show TCP/IP as 5 layers (Application, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical) — identical ideas, just with the Network Access layer split apart. Know both counts: 4 or 5.

sections.title: Encapsulation & Decapsulation
sections.html:
Encapsulation (sender): going DOWN the stack, each layer adds its own header around the data from above. Decapsulation (receiver): going UP, each layer strips its header and passes the payload up.

Figure 2. Encapsulation wraps data in layer-headers going down; decapsulation unwraps it going up.
Why?
Why is the Ethernet destination the router, not Google? Ethernet only works on the local network. Your laptop doesn't know (and can't use) Google's MAC address — so L2 delivers to the router, which forwards the IP packet to the next hop and builds a brand-new Ethernet frame for that leg.

sections.title: Headers, Payload & the Nesting Rule
sections.html:
HEADERcontrol information PAYLOADthe actual data being sent

Typical header contents: source & destination addresses (at that layer's scope), payload length, payload type/protocol, sequence numbers, error-check values, control flags (SYN, ACK…).

The nesting rule
Ethernet payload = IP packet  →  IP payload = TCP segment  →  TCP payload = HTTP message  →  HTTP payload = the webpage HTML

Figure 4. Ethernet II frame layout.
  • Preamble (7 B) + SFD (1 B) — synchronise the receiver's clock; SFD marks "real data starts after me".
  • Destination MAC (6 B) — Unicast one device · FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF broadcast to all · multicast for groups.

sections.title: MTU & IP Fragmentation
sections.html:
MTU — Maximum Transmission Unit: the largest payload a single frame can carry on a link.

Link typeMTULink typeMTU
Ethernet1500 bytesJumbo frames (data centre)up to 9000 B
Wi-Fi (in practice)1500 B (Ethernet-compatible)Loopback interface65536 B

If an IP packet exceeds a link's MTU, the IP layer fragments it. Example — 4500-byte payload over Ethernet (MTU 1500):

IP HdrFrag 1bytes 0–1479offset 0 · MF=1 IP HdrFrag 2bytes 1480–2959offset 185 · MF=1 IP HdrFrag 3bytes 2960–4439offset 370 · MF=1 IP HdrFrag 4bytes 4440–4499offset 555 · MF=0 (last)
Figure 5. One 4500-byte IP packet → four fragments (1480 bytes of data each + 20-byte header).
IP header fieldPurpose in fragmentation
IdentificationAll fragments of the same original packet share this 16-bit ID
Fragment OffsetWhere this fragment starts, in 8-byte units (13-bit field × 8 covers 65,528 B — enough for max IP size 65,535 B)
MF — More Fragments1 = more pieces coming · 0 = last fragment
DF — Don't Fragment1 = router must DROP (not fragment) if too large — used by PMTUD
Rules
Fragmentation can happen at any router whose MTU is smaller — but reassembly happens ONLY at the final destination. Lose even one fragment → destination discards all of them → source TCP retransmits the whole thing.

Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD) — how modern systems avoid fragmentation

1
Send with DF = 1
Packets marked "don't fragment".
2
Small-MTU router drops & reports
It returns ICMP "Fragmentation Needed, MTU = X".
3
Sender adjusts & retries
Repeats until the size fits the whole path — no fragments ever sent.
Gotcha
Firewalls that block all ICMP break PMTUD: large transfers (email attachments, image uploads) mysteriously hang while small ones succeed. Classic interview/troubleshooting trap.

sections.html:
A. Multiple Choice

Q1.MCQWhich OSI layer converts packets into frames for local delivery?
  • a) Network
  • b) Data Link
  • c) Transport
  • d) Physical
Q2.MCQThe EtherType value 0x0806 indicates the payload is:
  • a) IPv4
  • b) IPv6
  • c) ARP
  • d) VLAN tag
Q3.MCQA 4500-byte IP payload over Ethernet (MTU 1500) is split into:
  • a) 2 fragments
  • b) 3 fragments
  • c) 4 fragments
  • d) 5 fragments
Q4.MCQWhere are fragmented IP packets reassembled?
  • a) At the next router
  • b) At every router
  • c) Only at the final destination
  • d) At the nearest DNS server
Q5.MCQWhich fields change at every router hop (no NAT)?
  • a) Src & Dst IP
  • b) Src & Dst MAC and TTL
  • c) Ports
  • d) EtherType only

B. Short Answer (2–4 marks)

Q6.ShortDefine protocol. Why does networking use a layered architecture? (3 benefits)
Q7.ShortList the 7 OSI layers in order (both directions) with the mnemonic, and map them to the 4 TCP/IP layers.
Q8.ShortDraw and label the Ethernet frame with byte sizes. What is the FCS used for, and what happens on mismatch?
Q9.ShortDifferentiate frame, packet and segment (layer, address type, scope).
Q10.ShortWhat is MTU? Why does Ethernet enforce a 46-byte minimum payload?
Q11.ShortExplain the structure of a MAC address (OUI vs device ID) and its scope. Why do MACs change at each hop while IPs don't?

C. Long Answer (5–8 marks)

Q12.LongTrace encapsulation AND decapsulation for an HTTP GET from laptop (192.168.1.5) to google.com (142.250.195.46), naming every header added and every data-unit name at each layer. Explain why the Ethernet destination is the router's MAC.
Q13.NumericalAn IP packet with 4500 bytes of payload crosses an MTU-1500 link. Compute the number of fragments, each fragment's data range, fragment offset (in 8-byte units), and MF bit values. Which IP header fields make reassembly possible?
Q14.LongExplain Path MTU Discovery. Why does a firewall that blocks all ICMP cause "large uploads hang, small ones succeed"?
Q15.Long"Each layer treats the layer above as opaque payload." Explain this design principle and how it enables TCP to run unchanged over Wi-Fi, Ethernet or 4G.
Answer Key
A1. b — Data Link (L2) frames carry packets locally.
A2. c — 0x0806 = ARP (0x0800 = IPv4, 0x86DD = IPv6).
A3. c — ceil(4500/1480) = 4 fragments of ≤1480 data bytes.
A4. c — reassembly only at the final destination.
A5. b — MACs rewritten each hop; TTL decremented; IPs stay.
A6. Agreed rules: format, sequence, actions. Benefits: modularity, reusability, isolation (any three with one-line explanations).
A7. PDNTSPA; 5+6+7→Application, 4→Transport, 3→Internet, 1+2→Network Access.
A8. Figure 4 layout; FCS = CRC error check; mismatch → silent discard (TCP recovers later).
A9. Segment/TCP/ports/end-to-end · Packet/IP/IPs/host-to-host · Frame/Ethernet/MACs/one hop.
A10. Largest frame payload per link (1500 B Ethernet). 46-byte min → 64-byte min frame for collision detection on legacy shared Ethernet; smaller data is padded.
A11. 48-bit: 3-byte OUI (IEEE, manufacturer) + 3-byte device ID. Local scope only — each hop's frame is freshly built for that local leg; IPs provide the global end-to-end identity.
A13. 4 fragments: 0–1479 (off 0, MF1), 1480–2959 (off 185, MF1), 2960–4439 (off 370, MF1), 4440–4499 (off 555, MF0). Identification + offset + MF enable reassembly.
A12/A14/A15. Use Figures 2 & 5 and the PMTUD steps — graders award labelled diagrams and the "opaque payload" principle stated explicitly.
Wrap-Up — carry these into Lecture 3
Encapsulation
Every layer wraps the layer above: Data → Segment → Packet → Frame. Decapsulation reverses it at the receiver.
Two addresses
IPs identify hosts end-to-end and never change; MACs deliver on the local link and are rewritten at every hop.
MTU
1500 B Ethernet limit → packets larger than MTU−20 are fragmented; the receiver reassembles using ID + offset + MF.
Why layers win
TCP runs unchanged over Wi-Fi, Ethernet or 4G because each layer treats the one above as opaque payload.

title: IP Addresses and Subnetting — Part I
tagline: Why IP addresses exist, binary ↔ decimal fluency, network vs host ID, subnet masks, the AND trick, CIDR notation, public vs private ranges, and the loopback address.
summary: The single most exam-generating topic in the course: reading an IPv4 address like a router does. sections.title: Why IP Addresses?
sections.html:
MAC addresses (Lecture 2) only work locally — within one network segment. To route data across the Internet, across thousands of networks, we need a global addressing system. IP addresses provide:

Global uniqueness
Every public IP is unique world-wide — assigned by registries (IANA → regional registries → ISPs).
Hierarchy
The network portion enables routers to aggregate millions of destinations into few routing entries.
Logical & flexible
Reassignable in software — unlike the hardware-burned MAC.
Analogy
MAC = your name (travels with you, meaningless for postal delivery). IP = your postal address (hierarchical: city → street → house — exactly how routers narrow the search). A person can move houses (new IP) keeping the same name (MAC).

sections.title: Subnet Mask & the AND Operation
sections.html:
A subnet mask is a 32-bit number: 1s mark network bits, 0s mark host bits — and the 1s are always contiguous from the left.

Mask 255.255.255.0 in binary: 11111111.11111111.11111111.00000000 └──────── 24 network bits ────────┘└ 8 host bits ┘

The one calculation everything else builds on

Network Address = IP address AND Subnet Mask
AND: 1 AND 1 = 1 · anything AND 0 = 0 — the mask "keeps" the network part and zeroes the host part
IP: 192.168.1.5 → 11000000.10101000.00000001.00000101 Mask: 255.255.255.0 → 11111111.11111111.11111111.00000000 AND ────────────────────────┴────────┴────────┴──────── 11000000.10101000.00000001.00000000 = 192.168.1.0 Network address = 192.168.1.0 ← same for every device in this subnet!

Q12.LongExplain the structure of an IPv4 address with a diagram: octets, network portion, host portion, and how the subnet mask divides them. Why is the AND operation the natural way to find the network?
Q13.NumericalYou are given 192.168.1.5/24. Write the complete 32-bit binary of the address AND of its subnet mask, then compute the network and broadcast addresses.
Q14.ShortYour friend says "172.25.10.5 can't be private because it doesn't start with 10 or 192.168." Correct them precisely.
Answer Key
A1. c — 10.x.x.x is private; 172.32 is outside 172.16–31; 192.169 is outside 192.168.
A2. b — 2⁴−2 = 14.
A3. b — /26 blocks: 0, 64, 128, 192 → 77 sits in 64–127.
A4. b — APIPA self-assignment when DHCP fails.
A5. c — 240 = 11110000 → 28 ones.
A6. 172 = 128+32+8+4 = 10101100.
A7. Mask /16 keeps first two octets → 10.20.0.0.
A8. Network = the subnet's own identity (routers use it); broadcast = "all hosts here". Both are conventions every host must agree on — assigning them breaks addressing.
A9. Public = globally routable, registry-assigned, unique. Private = reusable internally, not routed on Internet. They exist because 4.3B addresses < devices on Earth — reuse + NAT (L11) stretches IPv4.
A10. 127.0.0.1 — packets never leave the machine. Uses: test the TCP/IP stack; run local dev servers (localhost:3000).
A11. /20 → mask 255.255.240.0; third octet 90 = 01011010 → keep 0101 → 01010000 = 80. Network 172.16.80.0, broadcast 172.16.95.255, hosts .80.1–.95.254, usable 4094.
A12. Use Figures 1 & 3; AND zeroes host bits because "anything AND 0 = 0" — leaving exactly the network identity all subnet devices share.
A13. 11000000.10101000.00000001.00000101 AND 11111111.11111111.11111111.00000000 → network 192.168.1.0, broadcast 192.168.1.255.
A14. The /12 private block is 172.16.0.0–172.31.255.255 — 172.25.x.x lies inside it, so it IS private. Private ≠ only 10/8 & 192.168/16.
Wrap-Up — carry these into Lecture 4
Anatomy
32 bits = 4 octets; the mask draws the line between network bits (shared identity) and host bits (who you are inside it).
AND to find home
IP AND mask = network address. "Anything AND 0 = 0" zeroes host bits, leaving exactly the subnet's identity.
Special addresses
All-host-bits-0 = network, all-ones = broadcast — never assign them. 127.0.0.1 talks to yourself.
Private blocks
10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16 are reusable inside networks; public addresses are globally unique. NAT (L11) bridges the two.
Next
Lecture 4 — IP Addresses & Subnetting II: borrowing host bits to carve subnets, VLSM, and the speed method that solves any paper question in 30 seconds.

sections.title: IPv6 — the 128-bit Future (Already Here)
sections.html:
• Why: IPv4 exhausted — IANA ran out of free blocks in 2011. IPv6 gives 2¹²⁸ ≈ 3.4×10³⁸ addresses — effectively unlimited.
  • Format: 128 bits written as 8 groups of 4 hex digits separated by colons:
    2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334
Compression Rule 1 — drop leading zeros
0db8 → db8  ·  0000 → 0
Compression Rule 2 — one :: for the longest zero-run
2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334
→ 2001:db8::8a2e:370:7334
Trap
:: may be used only once per address (two runs of zeros + :: would be ambiguous). If two runs exist, compress only the longer one (ties → the left one).

sections.title: Default Gateway — Direct or Forward?
sections.html:
The default gateway is the router's IP on your local network — the door to every other network. Your device makes a simple decision for every destination IP X:

1. Compute X AND my_subnet_mask 2. Result == my network address? YES → X is on my subnet → deliver directly (ARP for its MAC) NO → different network → send to default gateway (ARP for gateway's MAC)
Figure 1. The routing decision every host makes before touching the network.
Worked decision — my IP 192.168.1.5/24, gateway 192.168.1.1
To 192.168.1.20: .20 AND 255.255.255.0 = 192.168.1.0 == my network ✓ → direct To 8.8.8.8: 8.8.8.8 AND 255.255.255.0 = 8.8.8.0 ≠ my network → gateway

sections.title: NAT — Sharing One Public IP
sections.html:
The problem: your ISP gives you one public IP; your house has many devices. NAT (Network Address Translation) lets all of them share it, by rewriting IP:port pairs and remembering the mapping.

Figure 2. One public IP, many private devices — the router's NAT table keeps every conversation distinct by port.
Outgoing (SNAT)
Laptop: 192.168.1.5:52341 → 142.250.195.46:80 Router rewrites src: 203.0.113.5:10001 table: 10001 ↔ 192.168.1.5:52341
Reply comes back
Google → 203.0.113.5:10001 Router lookup 10001 → 192.168.1.5:52341 Delivers to laptop ✓
VariantDirectionUse case
SNAT (source NAT)OutgoingHome internet sharing
DNAT (destination NAT)IncomingPort forwarding, load balancing
PAT (Port Address Translation / overload)BothMany devices share one IP via distinct ports — what every home router does
Port forwarding (DNAT) — exposing a game server
Rule on router: public port 27015 → 192.168.1.10:27015 Friend connects to 203.0.113.5:27015 → router DNATs → 192.168.1.10:27015
Costs
NAT breaks end-to-end (inbound needs port forwarding), is stateful (router tracks every flow; reboot kills sessions), and confuses protocols that embed IPs in their payload (FTP, VoIP/SIP, some games).

sections.title: Networks as Graphs
sections.html:
A graph G = (V, E): V = routers (vertices/nodes), E = links (edges), and each edge carries a weight = link cost (latency, bandwidth-derived cost, or hop cost). Our running example — a 5-city network:

Figure 1. The running example graph used for every trace in this lecture.
adjacency list — sparse graphsJAVA
// Edge = (neighbour, cost). Map from node -> its edges. Map<String, List<Edge>> graph = new HashMap<>(); graph.put("Mumbai", List.of(new Edge("Delhi", 5), new Edge("Hyderabad", 3))); graph.put("Delhi", List.of(new Edge("Mumbai", 5), new Edge("Hyderabad", 2), new Edge("Chennai", 8))); graph.put("Hyderabad", List.of(new Edge("Mumbai", 3), new Edge("Delhi", 2), new Edge("Bangalore", 2))); graph.put("Chennai", List.of(new Edge("Delhi", 8), new Edge("Bangalore", 4))); graph.put("Bangalore", List.of(new Edge("Hyderabad", 2), new Edge("Chennai", 4))); // Edge is a tiny record: record Edge(String to, int w) {}

sections.title: BFS — Breadth-First Search
sections.html:
What BFS finds
The minimum hop-count path from source to every reachable node. Uses a queue (FIFO); explores layer by layer: 1 hop away, then 2 hops, then 3…
Limitation
BFS minimises hops, not cost. A 1-hop path costing 100 beats a 3-hop path costing 3 — wrong for cost-based routing. For cost, use Dijkstra (§4).
bfs with path trackingJAVA
static List<String> bfsPath(Map<String, List<Edge>> g, String start, String end) { Deque<List<String>> queue = new ArrayDeque<>(); Set<String> visited = new HashSet<>(); queue.add(List.of(start)); visited.add(start); while (!queue.isEmpty()) { List<String> path = queue.poll(); // FIFO — the queue is the whole trick String node = path.get(path.size() - 1); if (node.equals(end)) return path; // first visit = fewest hops for (Edge e : g.get(node)) { if (visited.add(e.to())) { List<String> next = new ArrayList<>(path); next.add(e.to()); queue.add(next); // carry the path alongside } } } return null; // end unreachable from start }
bfs with path trackingC++
vector<string> bfsPath(map<string, vector<pair<string,int>>>& g, string start, string end) { queue<vector<string>> q; set<string> visited; q.push({start}); visited.insert(start); while (!q.empty()) { auto path = q.front(); q.pop(); // FIFO — the queue is the whole trick string node = path.back(); if (node == end) return path; // first visit = fewest hops for (auto& [nb, w] : g[node]) { if (!visited.count(nb)) { visited.insert(nb); auto next = path; next.push_back(nb); q.push(next); // carry the path alongside } } } return {}; // end unreachable from start }

sections.title: DFS — Depth-First Search
sections.html:
DFS explores as deep as possible along one branch before backtracking — a stack (or recursion) instead of a queue. Finds a path, not necessarily the shortest. O(V+E).

dfs — iterative + cycle detectionJAVA
static List<String> dfsIterative(Map<String, List<Edge>> g, String start) { Deque<String> stack = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of(start)); Set<String> visited = new HashSet<>(); List<String> order = new ArrayList<>(); while (!stack.isEmpty()) { String node = stack.pop(); // LIFO — go deep first if (visited.add(node)) { order.add(node); for (Edge e : g.get(node)) if (!visited.contains(e.to())) stack.push(e.to()); } } return order; } static boolean hasCycle(String node, Set<String> visited, Set<String> recStack, Map<String, List<Edge>> g) { visited.add(node); recStack.add(node); // on the current path for (Edge e : g.get(node)) { if (!visited.contains(e.to())) { if (hasCycle(e.to(), visited, recStack, g)) return true; } else if (recStack.contains(e.to())) { return true; // back edge = cycle! } } recStack.remove(node); // leave the current path return false; }
dfs — iterative + cycle detectionC++
vector<string> dfsIterative(map<string, vector<pair<string,int>>>& g, string start) { stack<string> st; st.push(start); set<string> visited; vector<string> order; while (!st.empty()) { string node = st.top(); st.pop(); // LIFO — go deep first if (!visited.count(node)) { visited.insert(node); order.push_back(node); for (auto& [nb, w] : g[node]) if (!visited.count(nb)) st.push(nb); } } return order; } bool hasCycle(const string& node, set<string>& visited, set<string>& recStack, map<string, vector<pair<string,int>>>& g) { visited.insert(node); recStack.insert(node); // on the current path for (auto& [nb, w] : g[node]) { if (!visited.count(nb)) { if (hasCycle(nb, visited, recStack, g)) return true; } else if (recStack.count(nb)) { return true; // back edge = cycle! } } recStack.erase(node); // leave the current path return false; }
Trace — DFS from Mumbai
Visit Mumbai → push Delhi, Hyderabad Pop Hyderabad → push Bangalore Pop Bangalore → push Chennai Pop Chennai → Delhi already seen Pop Delhi → all neighbours visited Order: Mumbai → Hyderabad → Bangalore → Chennai → Delhi
Network uses of DFS
  • Topology discovery — walk every reachable router
  • Cycle detection — a cycle in the routing graph = a potential routing loop (packets circling forever)
  • Spanning-tree construction (preview of Lecture 6 / STP)

sections.title: Dijkstra — Minimum-Cost Paths
sections.html:
Idea
Greedy: always expand the cheapest unfinished node; relax its neighbours. A min-heap serves the cheapest node fast.
Guarantee
Optimal costs to ALL nodes — but only when all edge weights ≥ 0 (why: Lecture 6).
Complexity
O((V+E) log V) with a binary heap — the price of the priority queue, worth it for correct costs.
dijkstra + path reconstructionJAVA

sections.title: Why Dijkstra Fails on Negative Edges
sections.html:
Dijkstra's greedy assumption: once a node is finalised (popped), its shortest distance is correct. Negative edges break exactly this.

Figure 1. The classic counterexample — greediness + negative edges = wrong answer.

sections.title: Bellman-Ford — the Fix
sections.html:
Core idea: relax every edge, V−1 times. Each full pass propagates shortest paths at least one more hop further. Why V−1? Any shortest path (without a negative cycle) visits at most V−1 edges.

bellman-ford with negative-cycle detectionJAVA
// edges: (u, v, weight) — processing order doesn't matter! static Map<String, Integer> bellmanFord(List<Edge3> edges, Set<String> vertices, String src, Map<String, String> prev) { Map<String, Integer> dist = new HashMap<>(); for (String v : vertices) dist.put(v, Integer.MAX_VALUE); dist.put(src, 0); for (int i = 0; i < vertices.size() - 1; i++) { // V−1 passes for (Edge3 e : edges) if (dist.get(e.u()) != Integer.MAX_VALUE && dist.get(e.u()) + e.w() < dist.get(e.v())) { dist.put(e.v(), dist.get(e.u()) + e.w()); // relax prev.put(e.v(), e.u()); } } for (Edge3 e : edges) { // V-th pass = detector if (dist.get(e.u()) != Integer.MAX_VALUE && dist.get(e.u()) + e.w() < dist.get(e.v())) throw new IllegalStateException("Negative weight cycle detected!"); } return dist; }
bellman-ford with negative-cycle detectionC++
// edges: (u, v, weight) — processing order doesn't matter! map<string, int> bellmanFord(vector<Edge3>& edges, int V, string src, map<string, string>& prev) { map<string, int> dist; for (auto& [v, _] : dist) dist[v] = INT_MAX; dist[src] = 0; for (int i = 0; i < V - 1; ++i) { // V−1 passes for (auto& e : edges) if (dist[e.u] != INT_MAX && dist[e.u] + e.w < dist[e.v]) { dist[e.v] = dist[e.u] + e.w; // relax prev[e.v] = e.u; } } for (auto& e : edges) { // V-th pass = detector if (dist[e.u] != INT_MAX && dist[e.u] + e.w < dist[e.v]) throw runtime_error("Negative weight cycle detected!"); } return dist; }

Negative cycles = routing loops

Detected
If a V-th pass can still relax → a negative cycle exists (e.g. A→B(1)→C(−3)→A(1): each lap −1 → "shortest path" is meaningless). In networking, a negative cycle IS a routing loop — packets circulating forever. Bellman-Ford detects it; Dijkstra cannot.

sections.title: Minimum Spanning Tree (MST)
sections.html:
Spanning tree
Connects all vertices, has no cycles, exactly V−1 edges.
Minimum spanning tree
The spanning tree with the lowest total edge weight.
Two classics
Kruskal: sort edges, add if no cycle (union-find). Prim: grow tree from any node, always add cheapest outgoing edge.
kruskal — sort + union-findJAVA
static List<Edge> kruskal(List<Edge> edges, Set<String> vertices) { edges.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Edge::w)); // 1. sort by weight Map<String, String> parent = new HashMap<>(); vertices.forEach(v -> parent.put(v, v)); // 2. find with path compression (halving) ... find(String x) { while (!parent.get(x).equals(x)) { parent.put(x, parent.get(parent.get(x))); x = parent.get(x); } return x; } List<Edge> mst = new ArrayList<>(); for (Edge e : edges) { String ru = find(e.u()), rv = find(e.v()); if (!ru.equals(rv)) { // 3. different trees? merge (no cycle) parent.put(ru, rv); mst.add(e); } } return mst; // stops naturally at V−1 edges }
kruskal — sort + union-findC++
vector<Edge> kruskal(vector<Edge> edges, int V) { sort(edges.begin(), edges.end(), [](const Edge& a, const Edge& b) { return a.w < b.w; }); // 1. sort by weight vector<int> parent(V); iota(parent.begin(), parent.end(), 0); // 2. find with path compression (halving) function<int(int)> find = [&](int x) { while (parent[x] != x) { parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]; x = parent[x]; } return x; }; vector<Edge> mst; for (auto& e : edges) { int ru = find(e.u), rv = find(e.v); if (ru != rv) { // 3. different trees? merge (no cycle) parent[ru] = rv; mst.push_back(e); } } return mst; // stops naturally at V−1 edges }

MST in real networks — Spanning Tree Protocol (STP, IEEE 802.1D)

The problem
Ethernet switches with redundant links create loops — broadcast frames circulate forever (a "broadcast storm") and melt the LAN.
The fix
Switches run a distributed MST algorithm: redundant links are logically blocked, leaving a loop-free tree. If an active link fails, STP unblocks a spare — automatic failover.

sections.title: Distance Vector vs Link State — the Big Split
sections.html:
Distance Vector (Bellman-Ford based)
  • Each router knows costs to direct neighbours only
  • Periodically broadcasts its entire routing table to neighbours
  • Update rule: dist[dest] = min(dist[dest], cost_to_nbr + nbr_dist[dest])
  • Converges over many rounds; partial (local) view
  • Protocols: RIP, BGP (path-vector)
Link State (Dijkstra based)
  • Each router floods its local link state (neighbours + costs) to ALL routers
  • Every router builds the complete topology map
  • Every router independently runs Dijkstra → consistent results
  • Fast convergence; no count-to-infinity
  • Protocols: OSPF, IS-IS
FeatureDistance VectorLink State
Information sharedRouting table (distances)Link state (direct neighbours)
Algorithm basisBellman-FordDijkstra
Topology knowledgePartial (local view)Full (global view)
Convergence speedSlowFast
Bandwidth useLow (periodic small updates)High at first (flooding), then quiet
Loop riskCount-to-infinityNone (consistent full map)
ExamplesRIP, BGPOSPF, IS-IS
Exam
The one-liner that earns marks: "DV shares distances, LS shares topology." Everything else (convergence speed, loop behaviour, algorithms) follows from that single design difference.

AS
An Autonomous System = a network under one administrative control with a unique ASN: Google AS15169, Cloudflare AS13335, Jio AS55836, BSNL AS9829. IGPs (RIP/OSPF/IS-IS) run inside; BGP (EGP) runs between.

Bellman-Ford
Relax every edge V−1 times → handles negative edges; a further pass that still improves = negative cycle. Dijkstra has no such safety net.
MST

DV vs LS

Analogy
Routing = planning the highway map (surveying roads, updating the map). Forwarding = reading a signpost at each junction and turning. Drivers (packets) never see the map — only signposts.

What is a router?

  • Multiple network interfaces, each attached to a different network
  • A routing table: destination → next hop + interface
  • A routing engine (control plane) that learns routes
  • A forwarding engine (data plane) that processes packets at line speed

Exam
Router vs Switch: Switch = Layer 2, forwards by MAC, inside one LAN. Router = Layer 3, forwards by IP + routing table, between networks. Modern "home routers" bundle both (Lecture 11).

sections.title: Longest Prefix Match (LPM)
sections.html:
When a packet's destination matches multiple entries, the most specific (longest) prefix wins.

Worked lookup — destination 192.168.1.200
Table entryMatches?Bits matchedResult
192.168.0.0/16 via 10.0.0.1✓ (192.168.x.x ⊂ /16)16
192.168.1.0/24 via 10.0.0.2✓24
192.168.1.128/25 via 10.0.0.3✓ (.200 is in .128–.255)25★ WINNER
0.0.0.0/0 via 10.0.0.4✓ (matches everything)0
Decision: forward via 10.0.0.3 — 25 bits beat 24, 16 and 0.
Why LPM matters
It enables hierarchical routing: an ISP carries one route 10.0.0.0/8 for a million customers, while a customer with 10.45.0.0/16 gets the more specific (winning) route. Specific overrides general — that's also how BGP hijacks work (Lecture 8).

sections.title: Default Route & Static Routing
sections.html:
Default route — 0.0.0.0/0
Matches every destination (zero bits checked). The fallback when nothing else matches: "if in doubt, send here".
Who needs a default?
Home device → home router → ISP → Tier-2 → Tier-1. But a Tier-1 core router has NO default — it carries the full Internet table (900K+ routes) because there is nobody "above" it to default to.

sections.title: Packet Forwarding — Hop by Hop
sections.html:
At EVERY router, for EVERY packet: 1. Extract destination IP 2. Search routing table — Longest Prefix Match 3. Match? → forward to next hop via that interface 4. No match & no default? → DROP + ICMP "Destination Unreachable"
Figure 2. The forwarding decision loop — millions of times per second.
Complete trace — Laptop 192.168.1.5 → Server 10.50.20.100
Laptop→R1→R2→R3→Server
#WhereDecision (LPM)Frame MACs
1Laptop10.50.20.100 ∉ 192.168.1.0/24 → send to gateway 192.168.1.1Laptop → R1
2R110.50.0.0/16 → next hop 10.0.0.2 via eth1R1 → R2 (rebuilt)
3R210.50.0.0/16 → next hop 10.0.1.2 via eth1R2 → R3 (rebuilt)
4R310.50.20.0/24 directly connected → ARP for .100 → deliverR3 → Server (rebuilt)
5ServerPacket received — IP src/dst unchanged the whole way ✓
Key idea
No router knows the full path. Each knows only the next hop — yet the chain of local decisions carries the packet across the planet. That's the "hop-by-hop" principle (and why routing loops are so dangerous — next lecture).

What changes at each hop?

Header fieldChanges?Why
IP Source / DestinationNo (unless NAT)End-to-end identity
TTLYes — −1 per routerPacket with TTL = 0 is dropped + ICMP Time Exceeded — prevents infinite loops
Ethernet Src/Dst MACYes — rewrittenNew frame per hop (L2 is local-only)
TTL & traceroute
TTL starts at 64 (Linux/mac) or 128 (Windows). traceroute exploits it: send TTL=1 → router 1 drops & complains (revealing itself); TTL=2 → router 2 complains; … until the destination answers. That's how Lecture 12 maps paths.

sections.title: Distance Vector Routing
sections.html:
Every router: (1) knows costs to direct neighbours, (2) periodically sends its entire routing table to those neighbours, (3) updates using the Bellman-Ford rule:

dist[dest] = min( dist[dest], cost_to_neighbor + neighbor_dist[dest] )
distributed Bellman-Ford — "tell me your distances, I'll add my cost to reach you"

Each round, information travels one more hop — good news spreads at "one hop per round" speed.

sections.title: Count-to-Infinity — and the Four Fixes
sections.html:
Setup: A — B — C in a line. Normal state: B reaches C directly (1), A reaches C via B (2). Now the B–C link fails:

The failure (bad news travels slowly)
B detects failure → sets C = ∞ A's old table arrives: "C = 2 via me… " B thinks: via A → C = 1+2 = 3 ← WRONG (A's path went through B!) B tells A: C = 3 → A updates: 4 A tells B: 4 → B updates: 5 … …creeps up to 16 = unreachable (RIP's ∞)
Why it's absurd
A's route to C goes through B — so A can never offer B a shortcut. The routers keep "discovering" routes that route through each other: a transient routing loop where packets bounce A↔B until TTL kills them, and convergence takes minutes.
FixRuleEffect
1. Split HorizonNever advertise a route back on the interface you learned it fromA never tells B "I can reach C" — the loop never starts
2. Poison ReverseInstead of silence: advertise the route back as ∞ (16)Stronger — B pre-knows A has no independent path; instant convergence
3. Triggered UpdatesOn failure: flood "C = 16" immediately, don't wait 30 sShrinks the window where stale info circulates
4. Holddown TimerAfter poisoning, ignore claims that the route is reachable for N secondsPrevents a slow neighbour's stale table from resurrecting the dead route
Exam
The 8-mark version: "Explain count-to-infinity with a diagram and state its solutions." Draw A—B—C, show the failed link, walk the 3→4→5 numbers, then the four fixes with one-line mechanisms. This exact narrative is what graders look for.

sections.title: Link State Routing — OSPF
sections.html:
Idea: make every router see the same complete map, then let each run Dijkstra independently — no more neighbour-gossip.

1
Discover neighbours — Hello packets (every 10 s)
Agree on hello/dead intervals, area ID, authentication → become neighbours.
2
Build a Link State Advertisement (LSA)
"I am R1. Link to R2 costs 10, link to R3 costs 5."
3
Flood LSAs to ALL routers in the area
Every router assembles the same Link State Database (LSDB) — the full topology map.
4
Run Dijkstra (SPF) on the LSDB
Each router computes shortest paths from itself → identical conclusions → consistent, loop-free tables.
5
React to change
Link fails → new LSA floods immediately → SPF re-runs. Convergence in seconds (Lecture 6's LS table explains why this beats DV).
OSPF cost formula
cost = ref_bw / iface_bw
ref = 100 Mbps default → 100M:1 · 10M:10 · 1M:100 — slower links cost more
Areas — scaling OSPF
Big networks split into areas; LSAs flood within an area only. All areas attach to Area 0 (backbone); ABRs (Area Border Routers) summarize between areas.

sections.title: BGP — the Protocol Between Organisations
sections.html:
• An AS (Autonomous System) = one organisation's network with a unique ASN: Google AS15169, Cloudflare AS13335, Jio AS55836, BSNL AS9829.
  • BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) = the EGP exchanging routes between ASes. It's policy-driven: business contracts decide paths as much as distance.
  • Path-vector: each advertisement carries the full AS_PATH list of networks traversed:
Google announces: 8.8.8.0/24 AS_PATH: [15169] Tata re-advertises: 8.8.8.0/24 AS_PATH: [6453, 15169] Airtel re-advertises: 8.8.8.0/24 AS_PATH: [9498, 6453, 15169] # Loop prevention: your own ASN already in the path? → discard the route.
BGP best-path order (simplified)Meaning
1. Highest LOCAL_PREFYour own policy preference (business choice)
2. Shortest AS_PATHFewer organisations crossed
3. Lowest MEDNeighbour's hint about which entry point to prefer
4. eBGP over iBGPExternal routes preferred over internal
5. Lowest IGP metric to next hopCloser exit wins ties
eBGP vs iBGP
eBGP runs between different ASes (the Internet's stitching). iBGP spreads externally-learned routes inside your own AS so all border routers agree.
BGP hijacking (real world)
Announce someone else's prefix as more specific (a /24 beats their /16 — LPM again!). 2008: Pakistan Telecom announced YouTube's /24 → worldwide YouTube traffic landed in Pakistan. Defence: RPKI cryptographic route signing.

Convergence = all routers holding consistent, correct tables. Convergence time = how long after a change before that's true.

summary: Everything between "typing a name" and "seeing a page": why DNS exists, its three-tier hierarchy, the full 9-step resolution walk, record types and dig commands; then HTTP — message formats byte-by-byte, methods with idempotency/safety, status-code families, and how cookies + sessions put memory into a stateless protocol.
objectives: Explain why DNS exists and walk its hierarchy (root → TLD → authoritative)

sections.title: Why DNS?
sections.html:
DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-readable names (google.com) into IP addresses (142.250.195.46). Why not use IPs directly?

  • Memory: names beat dotted quads (especially IPv6 monsters)
  • Stability: servers change IPs; the name stays constant
  • Scaling: one name → many IPs (load balancing) · many users → nearest IP (CDN geo-routing)
Analogy
DNS = the Internet's phone book: you know the name ("Mom"), the phone book gives the number. And like a good contact app, everyone caches recently-dialled numbers so the book isn't opened every time.

sections.html:
Figure 1. A distributed tree: no single server knows everything — each level delegates downward.
Server typeKnowsExample
Root serversWhich servers run each TLD (13 logical identities A–M)Operated by ICANN, Verisign…

sections.title: Full Resolution — Step by Step
sections.html:
Query: browser needs the IP for www.google.com

1Browser cache
Fresh cached answer? Use it. Done — no network.
2OS cache + /etc/hosts
Local system-level cache and hosts file.
3Ask the recursive resolver
Query to configured DNS (router, ISP, 8.8.8.8) — UDP port 53.
4Resolver cache
Cached & TTL-valid? Instant answer. Else start walking.
5Resolver → ROOT server
Root: "Not me — the .com TLD is at 192.5.6.30." (referral)
6Resolver → .com TLD
TLD: "Ask Google's nameservers — ns1.google.com." (referral)
7Resolver → authoritative
ns1: "www.google.com = 142.250.195.46, TTL 300" (answer)
8–9Cache + return
Resolver caches for TTL seconds and returns the IP; browser connects to it.
Exam
Iterative vs recursive: the resolver does iterative walks (ask root, then TLD, then auth); your machine makes one recursive request ("get me the answer, however many steps it takes"). Draw the 9 arrows — it's a guaranteed diagram question.

Caching & TTL

  • Every record carries a TTL (seconds to cache); after expiry the resolver must re-ask.
  • Low TTL = fast changes, more queries · High TTL = fewer queries, slow propagation.

sections.title: HTTP — Request & Response
sections.html:
HTTP is text-based (human-readable), stateless (each request is independent), and request-response (client initiates, server responds).

HTTP/1.1 200 OK ← status line Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8 Content-Length: 4523 Set-Cookie: session=abc; HttpOnly; Secure Cache-Control: max-age=3600 ← blank line <!DOCTYPE html> <html>… ← body

Methods

Definitions + REST pattern
Idempotent = repeating gives the same result as once. Safe = changes nothing. REST: GET /api/users list · POST /api/users create · GET /api/users/42 one · PUT /api/users/42 replace · PATCH partial · DELETE remove.

sections.title: Cookies & Sessions — Memory for a Stateless Protocol
sections.html:
HTTP forgets you between requests. Cookies fix it: the server hands the browser a token; the browser returns it on every subsequent request — the server recognises the token and "remembers".

1 Login POST→2 Set-Cookie: session=abc→3 Browser stores→4 Cookie: session=abc (every request)→5 Server maps id → your session
AttributeEffect
HttpOnlyJavaScript can't read the cookie → blunts XSS token theft
SecureSent over HTTPS only → no plaintext interception
SameSite=StrictNever sent on cross-site requests → CSRF defence
Max-Age=NExpires after N seconds
Domain=.example.comShared across all subdomains
Cookie (client-side)Session (server-side)

Size~4 KBUnlimited

Exam
Authentication vs Authorization: authN = proving identity (login, 401 when missing); authZ = checking permission (403 when denied). And: servers store a session ID in the cookie — not your data — so a stolen cookie is a stolen identity but a leaked DB row doesn't leak sessions.

title: TCP, UDP and Socket Programming
tagline: The transport layer: ports and multiplexing, TCP vs UDP, the three-way handshake and four-way close, reliability, flow control, and real socket code in Java and C++.
summary: How one machine runs a hundred apps at once (ports), the full TCP-vs-UDP decision framework with real applications, byte-level handshake and close sequences, how TCP recovers losses (ACKs, timeouts, fast retransmit), how the sliding window prevents flooding, and working TCP/UDP client-server code in Java and C++ you can run tonight.
objectives: Explain the transport layer's role: ports, multiplexing, demultiplexing
Compare TCP and UDP and pick correctly per application

sections.title: Ports — Many Apps, One Machine
sections.html:
IP delivers to a machine; a machine runs many programs. A port (16-bit, 0–65535) identifies the process. Full address = IP : port (e.g. 192.168.1.5:52341). Multiplexing tags outgoing packets with source ports; demultiplexing delivers incoming packets to the right process by destination port.

RangeNameUseRangeNameUse
0–1023Well-knownHTTP 80 · HTTPS 443 · SSH 22 · DNS 53 · SMTP 251024–49151RegisteredMySQL 3306 · Redis 6379 · Postgres 5432
49152–65535EphemeralClient-side temporary ports— the pair (src port, dst port) identifies the conversation

sections.title: TCP — Reliable, Ordered, Controlled
sections.html:
TCP's four guarantees
Reliable (data arrives or sender knows) · In-order (bytes arrive as sent) · Error-checked (bad segments retransmitted) · Flow-controlled (never drowns the receiver).
Key header fields
Src/Dst Port (16b) · Sequence (32b — byte position!) · Acknowledgment (32b — next byte expected) · Flags (SYN ACK FIN RST PSH URG) · Window (16b — receiver buffer) · Checksum.

Three-way handshake (connection setup)

Figure 2. SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK. Why random initial sequence numbers? So stale packets from an old connection can't masquerade as new ones.

Four-way close (connection teardown)

Figure 3. Each side closes independently — FIN/ACK in each direction.

Reliability — ACKs and retransmission

Sender: [seq 1–1000] [seq 1001–2000] [seq 2001–3000] Receiver: [ACK 1001] [ACK 2001] ✗ LOST Then: [ACK 3001 arrives anyway…] Receiver keeps repeating: [ACK 2001] [ACK 2001] [ACK 2001] ← 3 duplicate ACKs Sender: FAST RETRANSMIT seq 2001 immediately (no waiting for timeout)
Two retransmission triggers
1. RTO timeout — no ACK within the retransmission timeout → resend. 2. Fast retransmit — 3 duplicate ACKs → resend immediately (much faster).
Flow control — sliding window
Every ACK carries a window size = "send up to N unacknowledged bytes". Big buffer → window 65535 → pipeline freely. Full buffer → window 0 → sender pauses (zero window).

sections.title: Socket Programming — Java & C++
sections.html:
A socket is the OS's endpoint abstraction: AF_INET (IPv4) × SOCK_STREAM (TCP) or SOCK_DGRAM (UDP).

SERVER CLIENT socket() socket() bind(('0.0.0.0', 8080)) listen(backlog) accept() ─────── 3-way ──────── connect() recv() ◀────── data ────────── send() send() ─────── reply ─────────▶ recv() close() ─────── 4-way ────────▶ close()
Figure 4. The client-server lifecycle — every socket program follows this dance.
tcp echo serverJAVA
import java.io.*; import java.net.*; try (ServerSocket server = new ServerSocket(8080)) { // bind + listen System.out.println("listening on 8080"); while (true) { Socket c = server.accept(); // blocks — handshake happens here var in = new BufferedReader( new InputStreamReader(c.getInputStream())); var out = new PrintWriter(c.getOutputStream(), true); String line = in.readLine(); out.println("Echo: " + line); c.close(); // 4-way close } }
tcp echo serverC++
int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); int yes = 1; setsockopt(server, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, &yes, sizeof(yes)); sockaddr_in addr{AF_INET, htons(8080), {INADDR_ANY}}; bind(server, (sockaddr*)&addr, sizeof(addr)); listen(server, 5); // backlog of 5 printf("listening on 8080\n"); while (true) { int c = accept(server, nullptr, nullptr); // blocks — handshake happens here char buf[1024] = {0}; read(c, buf, sizeof(buf)); string reply = string("Echo: ") + buf; write(c, reply.c_str(), reply.size()); close(c); // 4-way close }
tcp client + udp pairJAVA
// TCP client — the handshake happens inside connect() try (Socket client = new Socket("127.0.0.1", 8080)) { var out = new PrintWriter(client.getOutputStream(), true); var in = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(client.getInputStream())); out.println("Hello!"); System.out.println(in.readLine()); } // 4-way close // UDP server — no listen/accept at all try (DatagramSocket u = new DatagramSocket(9090)) { byte[] buf = new byte[1024]; DatagramPacket p = new DatagramPacket(buf, buf.length); u.receive(p); // + sender address u.send(new DatagramPacket("got it".getBytes(), 6, p.getAddress(), p.getPort())); } // UDP client try (DatagramSocket uc = new DatagramSocket()) { uc.send(new DatagramPacket("ping".getBytes(), 4, InetAddress.getByName("127.0.0.1"), 9090)); byte[] buf = new byte[1024]; DatagramPacket r = new DatagramPacket(buf, buf.length); uc.receive(r); System.out.println(new String(r.getData(), 0, r.getLength())); }
tcp client + udp pairC++
// TCP client — the handshake happens inside connect() int c = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); sockaddr_in a{AF_INET, htons(8080), {inet_addr("127.0.0.1")}}; connect(c, (sockaddr*)&a, sizeof(a)); // <- handshake write(c, "Hello!", 6); char buf[1024] = {0}; read(c, buf, sizeof(buf)); close(c); // 4-way close // UDP server — no listen/accept at all int u = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM, 0); sockaddr_in ua{AF_INET, htons(9090), {INADDR_ANY}}; bind(u, (sockaddr*)&ua, sizeof(ua)); char buf[1024]; sockaddr_in from; socklen_t fl = sizeof(from); recvfrom(u, buf, sizeof(buf), 0, (sockaddr*)&from, &fl); // + sender addr sendto(u, "got it", 6, 0, (sockaddr*)&from, fl); // UDP client int uc = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM, 0); sockaddr_in dst{AF_INET, htons(9090), {inet_addr("127.0.0.1")}}; sendto(uc, "ping", 4, 0, (sockaddr*)&dst, sizeof(dst)); recvfrom(uc, buf, sizeof(buf), 0, nullptr, nullptr);
Note
recv() returning 0 bytes on a TCP socket = the other side closed cleanly (this is how you detect FIN). To serve many clients at once, wrap each accepted client in a thread (or use asyncio selectors).

sections.title: TCP vs UDP — the Decision Table
sections.html:
FeatureTCPUDP
ConnectionConnection-oriented (handshake)Connectionless — just send
ReliabilityGuaranteed (ACK + retransmit)None — may lose, dup, reorder
OrderingGuaranteedNot guaranteed
Error detectionChecksum + retransmitChecksum only (detects, drops)
Header size20+ bytes8 bytes
Speed / overheadSlowerFaster
Flow controlYes (window)No
Use casesHTTP(S), SSH, email, databasesDNS, streaming, games, VoIP, DHCP, QUIC
Exam
"A live game leaderboard updates every 100 ms — TCP or UDP?" UDP: a missed update is stale in 100 ms anyway; retransmission adds nothing but delay. "File download?" TCP — every byte must arrive, in order.

sections.title: Important Questions — Exam Practice
sections.html:
A. Multiple Choice

Q1.MCQThe UDP header is exactly:
  • a) 20 bytes
  • b) 8 bytes
  • c) 4 bytes
  • d) 16 bytes
Q2.MCQIn the three-way handshake, packet 2 carries flags:
  • a) SYN only
  • b) ACK only
  • c) SYN+ACK
  • d) FIN+ACK
Q3.MCQFast retransmit triggers after:
  • a) 1 lost packet
  • b) RTO expiry
  • c) 3 duplicate ACKs
  • d) window = 0
Q4.MCQA window size of 0 means:
  • a) connection closed
  • b) sender must pause (receiver buffer full)
  • c) maximum speed
  • d) UDP fallback
Q5.MCQWhich socket call exists ONLY on the TCP server side?
  • a) socket()
  • b) bind()
  • c) listen()/accept()
  • d> sendto()
Q6.MCQTIME_WAIT lasts 2×MSL mainly to:
  • a) speed up closing
  • b) let a lost final ACK be answered by FIN-retransmit, and old duplicates die
  • c) free the port instantly
  • d) encrypt remaining data

B. Short Answer (2–4 marks)

Q7.ShortWhat problem do ports solve? Define multiplexing and demultiplexing.
Q8.ShortWhy does TCP randomise initial sequence numbers?
Q9.ShortWhy does the close need FOUR messages while open needs three?
Q10.ShortDifference between timeout retransmission and fast retransmit — which is faster and why?
Q11.ShortWhat does the Window Size field accomplish? What happens at 0?
Q12.ShortYour recv() returns b'' — what happened, and what should your code do?

C. Long Answer / Code (5–8 marks)

Q13.LongDraw and explain the three-way handshake and four-way close with sequence/acknowledgment numbers at every step. Include why TIME_WAIT exists.
Q14.CodeWrite a TCP echo server and its client in Java or C++ (any correct form). Annotate where the handshake and close occur.
Q15.CodeWrite a UDP server-client pair where the client sends a message and prints the server's reply. Why is there no accept()?
Q16.Long"TCP for correctness, UDP for speed." Justify with six applications (three each) and the mechanism differences behind the choice.
Answer Key
A1. b — 4 fields × 2 bytes.
A2. c — server's SYN+ACK.
A3. c — three dup-ACKs beat the timer.
A4. b — zero window = pause until reopened.
A5. c — listen/accept are TCP-server-only; UDP has bind→recvfrom.
A6. b — reliability of the close + duplicate expiry.
A7. Many processes per host; mux = tag outgoing with src port; demux = deliver by dst port.
A8. Prevents old-connection segments being accepted as valid data in a new connection (also raises spoofing difficulty).
A9. Each direction closes independently (half-close): FIN+ACK each way = 4 messages; open needs only agreement = 3.
A10. Timeout = wait for a full RTO; fast retransmit fires on 3 dup-ACKs, usually far sooner.
A11. Receiver advertises free buffer → bounds unacked in-flight bytes; 0 pauses sender.
A12. Peer sent FIN (closed cleanly) — close your socket / stop reading.
A14/A15. Compare with the §4 code: server thread-per-client with accept() in a loop; UDP has no accept because there is no connection — recvfrom returns the sender's address for the reply.
A16. TCP: web, file transfer, DB (every byte, in order). UDP: DNS, streaming, gaming (freshness > completeness). Mechanisms: ACK/retransmit/ordering/window vs none.
Wrap-Up — carry these into Lecture 11
TCP vs UDP
TCP = connection, reliable, ordered bytes. UDP = connectionless, 8-byte header, fast and fire-and-forget. Pick per-app, not "better".
Ports
0–1023 well-known, up to 49151 registered, rest ephemeral. Socket = IP:port; 80/443/53/22 worth memorising.
Handshake & teardown
SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK opens (seq x, x+1, y, y+1); FIN ×2 each direction closes. TIME_WAIT = 2×MSL.
Reliability engine
ACKs, retransmit (fast on 3 dup-ACKs), flow window from the receiver, congestion window from the network.

sections.html:
The gap: IP routes globally, Ethernet delivers locally by MAC. ARP bridges them: "which MAC owns this IP on my LAN?"

Figure 1. One broadcast question, one unicast answer, one cached mapping.
arp commandsterminal
arp -a # view cache (all OSes) ip neigh show # Linux preferred — shows STATE too ip neigh flush all # clear cache (root)
StateMeaningStateMeaning
REACHABLEconfirmed recently (~30 s)PROBEsending unicast re-checks
STALEunused; verify before next useFAILEDno answer → entry deleted
DELAYturned stale; probe pending—
Gratuitous ARP
A device ARPs for its own IP: (1) conflict detection — a reply means someone stole my IP! (2) cache refresh — announce a new/failovered MAC to everyone.
Proxy ARP
A router answers ARP on behalf of devices on other subnets — legacy trick to make distant hosts look local.

sections.title: DHCP — the DORA Dance
sections.html:
DHCP hands a joining device everything it needs: IP, subnet mask, default gateway, DNS server, lease time. It runs over UDP 67 (server) / 68 (client) — UDP because the client has no IP yet and needs broadcast (TCP can do neither).

Figure 2. DORA — Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge. REQUEST stays broadcast on purpose (declining other servers).

Lease renewal timeline

TimeEvent
T1 = 50% of leaseclient unicasts REQUEST to the original server ("renew me")
T2 = 87.5%no answer? broadcast REQUEST — any DHCP server may extend
T3 = 100%lease expires — IP lost; full DORA restarts (brief outage)
24-hour lease example
T1 at 12 h (unicast renew) → T2 at 21 h (broadcast) → T3 at 24 h (expire + re-DORA). Large networks with many subnets use DHCP relay agents on routers to forward broadcasts to a central server.

sections.html:
Sends packets with TTL = 1, 2, 3… Each router that kills a packet replies ICMP Time Exceeded — revealing itself. (Windows: tracert; better: mtr = traceroute + continuous stats.)

traceroute google.com   ·   traceroute -T -p 80 google.com (TCP, dodges ICMP blocks)
1 192.168.1.1 1.0 ms ← your gateway 2 10.50.0.1 8.2 ms ← ISP first hop 3 * * * ← ICMP filtered (traffic still flows!) 4 10.60.100.2 15.1 ms 5 72.14.239.45 18.4 ms ← Google peering 6 142.250.195.46 19.9 ms ← destination ✓
Reading it
Latency jumps locate congestion: hop4 at 200 ms after hop3 at 8 ms → the slow link is at hop 4. And * * * does not mean broken — many routers just rate-limit ICMP replies while happily forwarding your traffic.

Q14.LongExplain the TCP state machine story: LISTEN → SYN_SENT → ESTABLISHED → CLOSE_WAIT → TIME_WAIT, and what each stuck state diagnoses in a real application.
Q15.CodeWrite tcpdump commands: (a) capture DNS to a file without lookups, (b) watch SYN packets to port 80, (c) view plaintext HTTP bodies, (d) capture traffic between two hosts.

Answer Key
A1. b — IP works, name resolution doesn't.
A2. b — routers may rate-limit ICMP; forwarding continues.
A3. b — loopback bind accepts local connections only.
A4. b — remote closed, app never called close().
A5. b — authoritative "no such name".
A6. a — port 53 = DNS; -n disables reverse lookups.
A7. L1→L7 ladder; ip addr → ping GW → ping 8.8.8.8 → ping name → ss -tulpn → curl localhost:port.
A8. TTL=1,2,3… each zeroing router returns Time Exceeded; * * * = filtered/rate-limited ICMP, not failure.
A9. hops ≈ sending TTL (64 or 128) − received TTL (e.g. 64−57 = 7).
A10. Data arrived but the application hasn't read it — slow/hung app, or nowhere reading at all.
A11. Capture filters (tcpdump/BPF) limit what's recorded pre-capture; display filters (Wireshark) slice post-capture.
A12. At hop 4 — the jump appears crossing INTO hop 4 (its incoming link), since hop 3 responded quickly.
A13–A16. Ladder + checklist, state stories from §5, the four commands from §6, and PMTUD: blocked "Fragmentation Needed" ICMP = sender never learns to shrink packets.
Wrap-Up — carry these into Lecture 13
The ladder
Debug bottom-up: ip addr → ping GW → ping 8.8.8.8 → dig → curl/port. Each rung isolates one layer's failure.
States tell stories
SYN_SENT = no reply; CLOSE_WAIT = you forgot close(); TIME_WAIT = normal 2×MSL cool-down, not a leak.
Capture smart
tcpdump -n (no lookups) to record; Wireshark display filters to analyse. BPF limits what's captured, filters slice what's shown.
Silent failures
Blocked ICMP = PMTUD death: big uploads hang, small ones pass. traceroute's * * * = filtered ICMP, not always a failure.

sections.title: Phase 1 — Browser Cache (0 ms if lucky)
sections.html:
1
Memory cache
Same browsing session & fresh? Return instantly — zero network.
2
Disk cache
Within Cache-Control: max-age? Serve from disk. Stale? Send a conditional GET: If-None-Match: "etag123" → server replies 304 Not Modified → reuse cached body (no transfer!).
3
Miss → full journey begins
All the headers that make this work: Cache-Control (freshness), ETag (fingerprint), Expires (legacy).

sections.title: Phase 2 — DNS Resolution
sections.html:
Cache chain first: browser → OS → /etc/hosts → router forwarder (192.168.1.1:53) → recursive resolver (8.8.8.8) → hierarchy:

resolver → ROOT→"ask .com @ 192.5.6.30"→resolver → TLD→"ask ns1.example.com"→resolver → AUTH→93.184.216.34 · TTL 300
The DNS packet itself
UDP · src port 54321 (ephemeral) · dst port 53 · query type A — answer cached 300 s by every hop that touched it.

sections.title: Phase 3 — ARP the Gateway
sections.html:
Routing decision: 93.184.216.34 ∉ 192.168.1.0/24 → use gateway 192.168.1.1 ARP cache: hit → router MAC 11:22:33:44:55:66 (miss → broadcast + reply) Frame built: DstMAC router · SrcMAC laptop · IP 192.168.1.5 → 93.184.216.34
The rule
MACs change every hop; IPs persist end-to-end (until NAT rewrites them in Phase 4!).

sections.title: Phase 4 — TCP Handshake (+ NAT at the edge)
sections.html:
The handshake (to 93.184.216.34:443)
SYN (seq=x) → 1 RTT total ← SYN-ACK (seq=y, ack=x+1) ACK (ack=y+1) → ESTABLISHED
NAT happens right here
laptop: 192.168.1.5:52341 → 93.184.216.34:443 router: 203.0.113.5:10001 → 93.184.216.34:443 table: 10001 ↔ 192.168.1.5:52341

sections.title: Phase 5 — TLS 1.3 Handshake (1-RTT)
sections.html:
The messages
ClientHello → TLS 1.3 · cipher suites · SNI: www.example.com · random ← ServerHello + Certificate (+chain) + Finished Client Finished →  ENCRYPTED CHANNEL ✓
  • SNI — which domain's cert to serve (many sites per IP)
  • Certificate — public key + domain, signed up a chain to a trusted root CA
  • Forward secrecy — fresh ephemeral DH keys per session; leak later ≠ decrypt past
  • 0-RTT — returning clients send data immediately (replay-risk caveat)
Diffie-Hellman — the paint analogy
public: YELLOW paint Alice secret RED · Bob secret BLUE 1 Alice: Y+RED=ORANGE → sends 2 Bob: Y+BLUE=GREEN → sends 3 Alice: GREEN+RED=BROWN Bob: ORANGE+BLUE=BROWN Same colour — secret never travelled! Eve saw Y, O, G — can't unmix.
A=g^a mod p · B=g^b mod p · shared = g^(ab) mod p
attacker can't compute g^(ab) from g^a, g^b — discrete logarithm problem
Why TLS needs TCP
TLS gives confidentiality & integrity, not delivery. It still leans on TCP for reliable, ordered record transport — that's why it runs after the handshake, inside the connection.

sections.title: Phase 6 — The HTTP Request (encrypted)
sections.html:
the requestinside TLS
GET /products?id=42 HTTP/1.1 Host: www.example.com User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 … Accept-Encoding: gzip, br Cookie: session_id=abc123 Connection: keep-alive
packet stack leaving the laptopL7 → L2
HTTP GET L7 app TLS record (AES) L6 presentation TCP :52341 → :443 L4 transport IP .5 → .34 L3 network ETH MAC→MAC L2 link

sections.title: Phase 7 — Server Side: LB → App → Response
sections.html:
1
Load balancer
Terminates TLS (SSL offloading — backends see plain HTTP), picks a backend, adds X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.5 so the app logs the real client.
2
Web app
Route /products → auth via session_id → DB query → render HTML.
3
Response
200 OK · Content-Encoding: gzip · Cache-Control: max-age=300 · ETag · Set-Cookie (Secure; HttpOnly) — compressed body.

sections.title: Phase 8 — The Ride Home & Phase 9 — Close
sections.html:
LB re-encrypts → TCP src 93.184.216.34:443 → dst 203.0.113.5:10001 Router NAT reverse: 10001 → 192.168.1.5:52341 → LAN delivery Laptop: TCP reassembles → TLS decrypts → HTTP parses → gunzip → RENDER 🎉 Sub-resources reuse the same TCP connection (keep-alive / HTTP-2 multiplexing) Close: FIN → ACK → FIN → ACK → client TIME_WAIT ~60 s → NAT entry expires

The full timeline (typical, ~100 ms RTT to server)

0–5 msBrowser + OS cache misses
conditional checks fail — we must go to the network.
5–70 msDNS resolution
resolver → root → TLD → authoritative → 93.184.216.34.
70–75 msARP + SYN out
gateway MAC cached; SYN leaves, NAT entry created.
75–177 msTCP handshake
SYN-ACK back, ACK out — ESTABLISHED (1 RTT).
180–283 msTLS 1.3
ClientHello → ServerHello+cert → Finished (1 RTT).
285–400 msRequest + server work
GET travels encrypted; LB, app, DB do their thing.
400–500 msResponse arrives
decrypt, decompress, render HTML; 600–800 ms → CSS/JS/images done (often via CDN).
Optimisations
Second visit ≈ 50 ms because cache + keep-alive + session resumption skip DNS, handshake and most transfer. That's the exam's "why is the second load faster" answer, phase by phase.
