sections.title: Important Questions — Exam Practice
sections.html:
A. Multiple Choice

Q1.MCQA 304 Not Modified response means the browser sent:
  • a) Cache-Control: no-store
  • b) If-None-Match with an ETag
  • c) a fresh POST
  • d) nothing — server guessed
Q2.MCQTLS runs after the TCP handshake because:
  • a) DNS must finish first
  • b) TLS records need TCP's reliable, ordered transport
  • c) NAT requires it
  • d) certificates use UDP
Q3.MCQWhy does the load balancer add X-Forwarded-For?
  • a) speed
  • b) TLS encryption
  • c) preserve the real client IP after proxying
  • d) DNS
Q4.MCQOn the second visit to a page, which phases are typically skipped?
  • a) render only
  • b) DNS + full TLS (cache, keep-alive, resumption)
  • c) HTTP request
  • d) TCP close
Q5.MCQIf the NAT entry for an active TCP flow expires mid-stream:
  • a) nothing happens
  • b) return packets have no table entry → dropped; connection dies
  • c) TCP re-handshakes automatically
  • d) TLS renegotiates

B. Short Answer (2–4 marks)

Q6.ShortList the nine phases of an HTTPS request in order with one line each.
Q7.ShortWhy can't the browser skip the TCP handshake when TLS will encrypt anyway?
Q8.ShortWhat is SNI and what problem does it solve?
Q9.ShortExplain forward secrecy in one sentence using the paint analogy.
Q10.ShortWhat is TTFB and which two components make it up?
Q11.ShortWhy don't CSS/JS requests after the HTML need new handshakes?

C. Long Answer (5–8 marks)

Q12.LongThe big one: trace https://www.example.com end-to-end with a diagram — cache, DNS, ARP, TCP, TLS, HTTP, NAT, LB, response, close — naming the protocol, OSI layer and lecture for each phase.
Q13.LongExplain the TLS 1.3 handshake AND the Diffie-Hellman exchange (paint + math). Why can't an eavesdropper compute the session key?
Q14.LongReconstruct the ~500 ms timeline from this lecture and explain how caching, keep-alive and session resumption collapse it to ~50 ms.
Q15.Long"Everything in this course happens in one click." Prove it: map all 12 lectures to phases of the journey (table form), and identify the three most common failure points with tools.
Answer Key
A1. b — conditional GET with the cached ETag.
A2. b — TLS is a user of TCP's byte stream.
A3. c — otherwise logs/apps only ever see the LB's IP.
A4. b — cached resources, reused connection, resumed TLS.
A5. b — replies arrive at the public IP:port with no mapping → dropped.
A6. Cache → DNS → ARP → TCP → TLS → HTTP request → server/LB → response → close.
A7. TLS rides inside TCP; without the byte stream there is nothing to encrypt over.
A8. ClientHello carries the hostname so the server presents the right certificate — many HTTPS sites per IP.
A9. Fresh ephemeral keys per session mean a future private-key leak can't un-mix past sessions' colours.
A10. Time-to-first-Byte = network RTT + server processing (LB+app+DB).
A11. keep-alive reuses the established connection; HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over it.
A12–A15. The lecture IS the answer key — reproduce the phase diagram + mapping table + timeline with the optimisation column.

sections.title: Subnetting Drill (do all 10, then check)
sections.html:
The problems
  1. 10.20.30.40/16 → network? broadcast?
  2. 192.168.1.77/26 → network? usable range?
  3. 172.16.90.77/20 → mask? network? usable count?
  4. Need 50 hosts → prefix? usable?
  5. Need 500 subnets from /16 → new prefix? hosts each?
  6. How many /28s in a /24?
  7. 172.25.10.5 — public or private?
  8. 172.32.10.5 — public or private?
  9. 192.168.10.130/25 → network? broadcast?
  10. 10.45.60.100/20 → network? broadcast?
Answers
  1. 10.20.0.0 · 10.20.255.255
  2. 192.168.1.64 · .65–.126 (bc .127)
  3. 255.255.240.0 · 172.16.80.0 · 4094
  4. /26 · 62
  5. /25 · 126 each (2⁹=512 subnets)
  6. 16
  7. Private (172.16–31)
  8. Public — outside /12!
  9. 192.168.10.128 · .255
  10. 10.45.48.0 · 10.45.63.255
The 30-second method — worked on drill #3 (172.16.90.77/20)
  1. Block size from the octet that changes: /20 → third octet keeps 4 prefix bits → block = 2⁸⁻⁴ = 16 → boundaries 0, 16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96…
  2. Network: largest boundary ≤ 90 → third octet 80 → 172.16.80.0.
  3. Broadcast: next boundary − 1 → 96 − 1 → 172.16.95.255.
  4. Usable: .80.1 – .95.254 → host bits = 12 → 2¹² − 2 = 4094.
Traps that cost marks
"Usable" excludes network + broadcast (−2, always). 172.32 is public (outside 16–31). /31 and /32 have no usable hosts. Count subnets with 2^borrowed, hosts with 2^remaining − 2 — don't mix them.
Sanity checks
Network + block ≤ next network. Broadcast = network + block − 1. First usable = network + 1. If your broadcast crosses the next boundary, your block size is wrong — recount the borrowed bits.

19. Order Delhi(0) → Hyderabad(2) → Bangalore(4) → Mumbai(5) → Chennai(8); Delhi→Chennai = Delhi→Hyd→Bang→Chen (8).
20. B sets C=∞; A's stale "C=2" arrives → B:3 → A:4 → … to 16; cures: split horizon, poison reverse, triggered updates, holddown.
